newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Speaker links tax abatements to rent rules.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Speaker links tax abatements to rent rules.

text.p: New York State Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, has proposed offering landlords tax abatements as part of his effort to get them to accept the continuation of rent regulations for apartments.

"I'm just saying we ought to discuss the overall area of housing," Silver told reporters in Albany Tuesday when asked if he were linking property tax abatements outside the city to the expiry of rent rules on June 15.
He added, "I'm just saying, there are issues within it that are linking. The overall issue is housing, and there's nothing inappropriate about having an overall housing discussion."

The Speaker noted the Assembly's budget includes $650 million for property tax relief, though this plan has been faulted by a Pataki Administration aide for not setting forth in detail how this program would work.
In a prepared statement, Silver added the amount the Assembly had earmarked was $100 million more than Gov. George Pataki had proposed.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that the Assembly Speaker proposed increased subsidies for landlords, who have been fighting to get rent regulations ended.

The Assembly has approved a bill that would make the present system permanent, but the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, has threatened to let the rules expire unless there is agreement on a bill to return apartments to the free market system, while protecting the elderly, disabled and needy.

Bruno, in prepared remarks, attacked Silver for connecting rent rules and property tax relief. "The speaker is wrong to equate and link continuing rent regulatons with providing property tax relief. The proposals by the Senate and Gov Pataki to cut school property taxes would allow property owners to keep more of their own money. It is clearly not a subsidy."

Both Gov. Pataki and the Senate have proposed plans to make big cuts in property taxes, but the battle over the rent rules, which mainly affect New York City because it has the lion's share of the state's rent-regulated apartments, has delayed the budget, which was due on April 1, as well as efforts to reach agreements in other areas, from property tax cuts to welfare.
